What went terribly wrong is that white supremacist James von Brunn allegedly walked into the museum and started firing his rifle, shooting security officer Stephen Johns in the chest. Despite their initial shock, Weeks and McCuiston kept their composure enough to draw their weapons and start shooting at von Brunn, 88. Weeks had fired his gun in the line of duty 25 years earlier as a Washington, D.C., police officer. But he said nothing compared to this bloody confrontation. "This was terrible," Weeks said softly. "This was worse. ... We lost Officer Johns." Johns died shortly after the shooting, leaving behind a family that includes a teenage son who told CNN affiliate WUSA-TV the day after the tragedy that his dad was "my hero." Watching a video clip of those comments, McCuiston started crying. "First thing I thought about, I have an 11-year-old," the officer said before breaking down.  Watch the officers tell their story » . Just moments before their joint interview with CNN on Thursday, McCuiston and Weeks attended a grief counseling session together, and both men say they are still struggling with their emotions. The security officers said they believe von Brunn will survive his wounds and eventually face trial. So they would not discuss details of the shootout out of a fear of jeopardizing the criminal investigation, but they were willing to discuss their memories of Johns so that the public knows more about him. McCuiston said the 6-foot-6-inch, 300-pound Johns was a "gentle giant" who was always friendly to colleagues and museum visitors. "Just an awesome guy," he recalled. "Grin from ear to ear. You'd never know that man probably ever had a bad day in his life." Weeks said he wanted the world to see "what a man of hate did to this family, and the grief he caused. Let's all remember Officer Johns, and his family, because he took the ultimate -- he did his job and he was where he was supposed to be -- and the family suffered. That could have been anyone." McCuiston and Weeks, however, deflected suggestions that they may be heroes as well because if they had not stopped von Brunn, there's no telling how many of the more than 2,000 people visiting the museum at the time could have been injured or killed. "A lot of people are going to be saying what they have been saying, 'You are a hero, you're this, you're that,' " McCuiston said. "It's like we tell everybody, 'We chose this job, it's a job. " Johns' funeral on Friday has been moved to a larger church in the Washington area to accommodate all of the people who want to attend, and the museum will be closed most of the day so that his colleagues can attend. "Everyone knows when you lose someone, death is one of the worst things, even though it is reality," McCuiston said. "Time will hopefully heal all, and hopefully there will be a little bit of closure with us and the family and we can all just move forward but never forget what a wonderful man he was."

Von Brunn immediately raised a rifle and shot Johns in the chest at point-blank range.

"Stephen didn't even have a chance to draw his weapon," one officer recalled during the interview, visibly moved as he described the suddenness of the assault. "He was just doing his job, being polite, welcoming people to a place built on memory and peace."

Despite the shock of seeing their teammate fall, the surviving officers reacted within seconds. Officer Harry Weeks and fellow security personnel returned fire, striking von Brunn in the face and neutralizing the threat before he could advance further into the crowded museum, which was filled with hundreds of visitors, including school children.

"People called us heroes, but it didn't feel like a victory," another officer told CNN. "We did what we were trained to do, but we lost a brother. You carry that with you every single day."

They emphasized that while von Brunn acted alone that day, his actions were fueled by an ideology of hatred that remains a potent threat today. 

Reflecting on the location of the attack, the officers noted the stark irony of a hate crime occurring at an institution dedicated to teaching the world about the dangers of unchecked hatred and anti-Semitism.

"The museum stands to remind people where hate leads," one officer remarked. "Stephen’s sacrifice became a part of that lesson. We can never forget him, and we can't afford to ignore the hatred that brought that man to our doors."

Von Brunn was injured in the shootout and charged with first-degree murder and hate crimes. He died in prison in January 2010 while awaiting trial.

**WASHINGTON —** The heavy glass doors of the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum are open to the public once again, but for the officers who guard them, the air inside remains thick with a lingering, heavy grief. 

Weeks after an 88-year-old white supremacist opened fire in the museum’s crowded lobby, the physical damage has been repaired. The glass has been replaced, and the police tape is gone. But inside the security office, the silence left by 39-year-old Special Police Officer Stephen Tyrone Johns is deafening.

For surviving Officers Harry Weeks and Jason McCuiston, the split-second ambush on a quiet Wednesday afternoon changed everything. They are credited with saving countless lives by returning fire and neutralizing the gunman before he could push deeper into the museum. Yet, in the quiet aftermath, both men are struggling to reconcile the public praise they receive with the profound loss of their comrade.

### A Gentle Giant Remembered

To the millions of visitors who pass through the museum each year, Stephen Johns was a tall, reassuring presence at the entrance. To Weeks and McCuiston, he was "Big Steve"—a soft-spoken, 6-foot-6 family man known for his warm smile, his love of basketball, and his ability to lighten the mood in a building dedicated to one of history’s darkest chapters.

"Stephen was the front line of this place, not just for security, but for humanity," recalled Officer Harry Weeks, his voice tightening as he stood near the lobby where the shooting occurred. "He held the door open for people. He greeted them. That’s what he was doing when... when it happened. He was doing his job with grace."

On June 10, when the gunman walked up to the entrance with a vintage rifle raised, Johns had no time to draw his weapon. He took the initial blast at point-blank range. 

"It happened in a heartbeat," Weeks said, fighting back tears. "You train for the worst-case scenario, but nothing prepares you to see your brother go down right next to you. I think about those few seconds every single night when I close my eyes."

### The Instinct to Fight, The Struggle to Heal

Following the opening shot, McCuiston and Weeks reacted instantly, drawing their sidearms and engaging the shooter. Their rapid response brought the assailant down in the doorway, preventing what federal authorities said could have been a catastrophic mass shooting inside the crowded museum.

Despite their decisive action, Officer Jason McCuiston says the adrenaline of that day has long since faded, replaced by an overwhelming emotional fog and the heavy weight of survivor’s guilt.

"People talk about tactical response and split-second decisions, but in that moment, it’s just instinct and horror," McCuiston said. "We did what we were trained to do. We stopped the threat. But we couldn't save Stephen. That’s the part that sticks with you. You replaying it over and over—*what if I moved a second faster? What if we were standing in different spots?*"

Both officers admitted that returning to work has been an arduous process. Walking past the spot where Johns fell serves as a constant, painful reminder of the fragility of life and the stark reality of the hatred their institution works to educate against.

"It’s surreal," McCuiston added. "This museum exists to teach the world about the dangers of hate. And then hate walked right through our front door and took Stephen."

### The Burden of Being Called "Heroes"

In the days following the attack, local officials, national leaders, and members of the public showered Weeks, McCuiston, and the museum's security force with accolades. Flower memorials piled up outside the building, and letters of gratitude poured in from across the globe.

Yet, for the surviving officers, the label of "hero" feels less like an honor and more like an uncomfortable burden.

"I cringe a little every time someone calls me a hero," Weeks admitted candidly. "I don't feel like a hero. I feel like a guy who went to work with his friend, and only one of us walked out at the end of the shift. How can you feel like a hero when you lost a brother?"

McCuiston echoed those sentiments, emphasizing that any title of heroism belongs solely to the man they lost.

"If anyone is a hero, it’s Stephen," McCuiston said, looking toward a framed photograph of Johns that now sits in the staff area. "He absorbed the blow. He took the brunt of that evil so that dozens of visitors—children, families, tourists—could run to safety. We’re just the ones left behind to tell the story and carry his memory."

### Moving Forward

As the museum resumes its normal operations, the security team is trying to find a path forward. Counseling sessions, support from the law enforcement community, and the shared bond among the officers are helping, but the healing process promises to be long.

For Weeks and McCuiston, honoring Johns means continuing the work he died doing. They stand at their posts with a renewed sense of purpose, acutely aware of the solemn responsibility that comes with protecting a shrine to human memory and resilience.

"We come back to work every day for Stephen," Weeks said softly. "We stand tall because he stood tall. We aren't going to let hate win here. That’s how we honor him."
